claims.text: An ML potential trained on a minimal but representative set of ab initio molecular-dynamics data from solid and liquid states near fusion can support thermodynamic integration.
The proposed ML-accelerated integration can reproduce the full phase free-energy landscape, including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed method will cost substantially less than explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
CoCrFeMnNi is proposed as a prototypical multicomponent high-entropy-alloy test system near melting.
The relevant CoCrFeMnNi states comprise chemically disordered solid and liquid phases.
The ML training data will be obtained from a limited number of high-temperature ab initio MD simulations containing both solid and liquid configurations.
An ML interatomic potential can accurately interpolate the potential-energy surface across the complex configurational space of a multicomponent HEA.
The ML potential can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
Training on targeted ab initio MD configurations from both phases will produce energy and force predictions with near-first-principles accuracy.
Using the trained potential in thermodynamic integration will recover solid–liquid free-energy differences without the cost of carrying out the full workflow with ab initio MD.
The resulting free-energy differences will agree with explicit ab initio MD to within a few meV per atom.
The method will achieve a tenfold to hundredfold computational speedup relative to explicit ab initio MD.
The method will scale better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The intended validity domain is multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures.
Accuracy may deteriorate when relevant configurations lie outside the limited ab initio training set.
Rare or subtle configurations may contribute significantly to entropy and thereby affect calculated free-energy differences.
Discrepancies greater than 5 meV per atom in phase free energies or greater than 5% in melting temperature relative to independent explicit ab initio MD will falsify the hypothesis.
